title: Cracking Ice Age Horse Bones
place: Arroyo Seco 2, near Tres Arroyos, Buenos Aires Province, Argentina
text: About 14,000 years ago, people camped on a low knoll between a lake and a creek near today's Tres Arroyos, on Argentina's Pampas. They left quartzite tools carried from hills 110 km away, along with bones of giant ground sloths, toxodons and extinct horses. One horse leg bone shows two hammerstone blows from cracking it while fresh. Oddly, no spear points turn up in these early layers.

source.name: PLOS ONE: The Arroyo Seco 2 Site and Its Significance for the Peopling of the Americas

title: A Lord Buried With Whale-Tooth Earrings
place: El Caño Archaeological Park, Coclé, Panama
text: Around 1,200 years ago, a Coclé lord of about 30 was laid face down on top of a woman's body in a tomb at El Caño, Panama. As many as 31 other people may have been sacrificed to go with him. His grave goods included crocodile-shaped earrings, gold-covered sperm whale teeth, bone flutes, two bells and skirts made of dog teeth.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: 1,200-Year-Old Lord's Tomb Unearthed in Panama

title: Four Children Rewrite Cameroon's Past
place: Shum Laka rock shelter, Grassfields, Northwest Region, Cameroon
text: About 8,000 years ago, two boys were buried together in Shum Laka rock shelter in Cameroon's Grassfields, the younger lying across the older one's legs. Two more children were buried there about 3,000 years ago. Each pair were close relatives, and DNA shows all four were most like West-Central African hunter-gatherers, not today's local people. The older boy carried an extremely rare, deep Y-chromosome line called A00.

source.name: Nature (PMC): Ancient West African foragers in the context of African population history

title: Drowned Salt Kitchens of the Maya
place: Paynes Creek salt works, Punta Ycacos Lagoon, Toledo District, Belize
text: Between about 600 and 900 CE, Maya workers in Belize's Punta Ycacos Lagoon boiled brine in clay pots inside pole-and-thatch kitchens, making salt for inland cities. Rising seas later drowned more than 100 of these salt works, and mangrove peat preserved their wooden posts. Wear on their stone knives shows most were used to cut fish or meat, hinting that salted fish travelled inland too.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Salt and marine products in the Classic Maya economy from use-wear study of stone tools

title: Africa's Oldest Funeral Pyre
place: Hora 1 rock shelter, Mount Hora, Mzimba District, Malawi
text: About 9,500 years ago, hunter-gatherers at Hora 1 rock shelter in northern Malawi gathered at least 30 kg of deadwood and grass and cremated a small adult, probably a woman. It is Africa's earliest known intentional cremation. Cut marks show her body was first taken apart, and her skull is missing, perhaps kept for later rituals. Stone points lay among the burnt bones.

source.name: Science Advances (PMC): Earliest evidence for intentional cremation of human remains in Africa

title: Deer and Guinea Pig Above Bogotá
place: Tequendama rock shelter, Sabana de Bogotá, Cundinamarca, Colombia
text: About 13,000 years ago, hunter-gatherers began using Tequendama rock shelter, 2,570 m up on the Sabana de Bogotá in Colombia's Andes. Bones from its oldest layers come from white-tailed deer and guinea pigs. People kept returning for over 10,000 years. Chemical signatures in later skeletons show a diet built on C3 plants and animals, while at nearby Aguazuque maize shows up in bones around 4,400 years ago.

source.name: iScience (PMC): Human dietary diversity in the Colombian Andes at the terminal Pleistocene-late Holocene sites Tequendama and Aguazuque

title: Ancient Smelting Smoke Frozen in Andean Ice
place: Nevado Illimani, Cordillera Real, La Paz Department, Bolivia
text: Around 700 BCE, copper pollution starts showing up in the ice of Nevado Illimani, a 6,300-metre Bolivian peak. Scientists who drilled a 138.7 m ice core there linked it to early metalworkers such as the Chiripa culture around Lake Titicaca. Surprisingly, Inca and colonial-era copper levels were lower than these early peaks, and Andean copper smelting began about 1,200 years before widespread silver working.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Ice-core evidence of earliest extensive copper metallurgy in the Andes 2700 years ago

title: The Caribbean's Oldest Campsite
place: Banwari Trace, near Penal, Oropuche Lagoon, Trinidad and Tobago
text: About 7,900 years ago, people from the South American mainland were already camping at Banwari Trace in southern Trinidad, long counted as the oldest known archaeological site in the West Indies. Their shell midden holds bone points used as arrow tips and fish spears, fishhooks made from bevelled peccary teeth, and double-pointed bone hooks for fishing lines. A crouched skeleton found here in 1969 became known as Banwari Man.

source.name: University of the West Indies: Banwari Trace

source2.name: Latin American Antiquity: Geochronology and Paleoenvironmental Framework for the Oldest Archaeological Site (7800-7900 cal BP) in the West Indies, Banwari Trace, Trinidad

title: Snail-Shell Pendants From 1,500 km Away
place: Baño Nuevo 1 cave, Ñirehuao River valley, Aysén, Chile
text: Around 2,900 years ago, hunter-gatherers using Baño Nuevo cave in Chile's Aysén region wore pendants cut from the shell of a big land snail, Megalobulimus. The nearest place that snail lives is at least 1,500 km to the northeast. Wear marks suggest the pendants were tied or sewn onto something, not hung as necklaces. The cave, 100 km from the sea, also held beads made from keyhole limpet shells.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Long-distance transport of exotic shell personal adornments in Central West Patagonia: Baño Nuevo 1

title: A Spider Monkey Sent as a Gift?
place: Plaza of the Columns, Teotihuacan, State of Mexico, Mexico
text: Around 250 to 300 CE, a young female spider monkey was buried alive in the Plaza of the Columns at Teotihuacan, beside a golden eagle and rattlesnakes. Born somewhere humid, she spent at least two years captive in the dry central highlands, eating maize and chili. It is the earliest known captive primate in the Americas, and archaeologists think she was a diplomatic gift linked to Maya lords.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Earliest evidence of primate captivity and translocation supports gift diplomacy between Teotihuacan and the Maya

title: Axe-God Pendants and Fake Jade
place: Greater Nicoya region, Guanacaste, Costa Rica
text: By about 500 BCE, people in Costa Rica were carving 'axe-god' pendants from green stone, and by around 300 BCE jadeitite appears, probably brought from Guatemala's Motagua Valley. A study of 926 greenstone objects found jadeitite in about a quarter of Greater Nicoya's pieces, but many supposed jades are really green quartz, which looks almost identical. A raw jadeitite block from Las Huacas shows some was carved locally.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Greenstone artifacts in pre-Columbian Costa Rica: from raw material to local and interregional exchanges

title: Amazon Macaws Carried Over the Andes
place: Uhle Cemetery, Pachacamac, Lurín Valley, Lima, Peru
text: Sometime between about 1000 and 1400 CE, the Ychsma people buried feather-decorated bundles in a tomb at Pachacamac, on Peru's dry central coast. DNA shows the feathers came from Amazonian scarlet, red-and-green and blue-and-yellow macaws and mealy parrots. The birds' high genetic diversity suggests they were caught wild, carried alive across the Andes, then probably fed maize on the coast for a while.

source.name: Nature Communications (PMC): Ancient DNA and spatial modeling reveal a pre-Inca trans-Andean parrot trade

title: A Painting of the Fever Year
place: Buenos Aires, Argentina
text: In 1871, yellow fever killed about 14,000 people in Buenos Aires, a city of roughly 180,000. That same year Uruguayan painter Juan Manuel Blanes captured the tragedy on a canvas over two metres tall: a dead mother on a stone floor, her orphaned child beside her. In the background stand lawyer José Roque Pérez and Dr Manuel Argerich, volunteers who later died from helping the sick.

source.name: Emerging Infectious Diseases (PMC): Yellow Fever in Buenos Aires

title: The Student Who Infected Himself
place: Dos de Mayo Hospital, Lima, Peru
text: On 27 August 1885, in a Lima hospital, Peruvian medical student Daniel Carrión cut his arm and rubbed in blood from a verruga, the wart-like skin lesion of a mysterious Andean disease. He wanted to record its early symptoms. When he grew too weak to keep his diary, classmates carried on. He died on 5 October, having shown that verruga and Oroya fever were one disease, now named after him.

source.name: Emerging Infectious Diseases (CDC), June 2010: Photo Quiz on Daniel Carrión

source2.name: Revista Peruana de Medicina Experimental y Salud Pública (PMC): Chilean physicians and the study of Peruvian wart, a critical review

title: Stone Toolmakers on a Mozambique Hilltop
place: Chessungalane, near the Save River, Inhambane Province, Mozambique
text: About 23,000 years ago, Stone Age people began working stone on a flat-topped hill 12 km north of the Save River in Mozambique. They returned on and off until about 7,000 years ago, flaking quartz from the hill's gravels into simple tools and, in the last phase, using scarcer chert to make tiny bladelets. Found in 2023, Chessungalane is the first Stone Age site in Mozambique studied in such detail.

source.name: African Archaeological Review (PMC): Lithic Techno-economics and OSL Chronology of the Later Stone Age at Chessungalane, Save River Valley, Mozambique

title: Nine Thousand Years, Same Ancestors
place: Oakhurst rock shelter, near George, Western Cape, South Africa
text: About 10,000 years ago, a person buried in Oakhurst rock shelter near George, South Africa, left the oldest human DNA yet recovered from the country. Genomes from people buried there over the next 9,000 years show the same local hunter-gatherer ancestry, even as stone-tool styles changed. Across southern Africa, herder and farmer ancestry from farther north only reshaped the gene pool after about 1,300 years ago.

source.name: Nature Ecology & Evolution (PMC): 9,000 years of genetic continuity in southernmost Africa demonstrated at Oakhurst rockshelter

title: Stone Toolmakers Deep in a Gabon Cave
place: Pahon Cave, near Lastoursville, Ogooué-Lolo, Gabon
text: Between about 7,500 and 2,500 years ago, people repeatedly came 50 m inside Pahon Cave, in the dense rainforest of central Gabon. They knapped chert and quartz into small tools and left remains of giant African snails, freshwater crabs, porcupines, bushpigs and duikers. Bats, including fruit bats, make up most of the identified bones. A broken polished axe or adze turned up too.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Pahon Cave, Gabon: New insights into the Later Stone Age in the African rainforest

title: Cowpeas, Cattle and a Painted Wall
place: Kakapel rock shelter, Chelelemuk Hills, Busia County, Kenya
text: About 2,300 years ago, Early Iron Age people at Kakapel rock shelter, at the foot of Mount Elgon in western Kenya, left behind cowpeas, along with a cattle bone of about the same age. Hunter-gatherers making Kansyore pottery had used the shelter for thousands of years before. Its rock-art panel, painted in red and white over different periods, shows people, antelopes, buffalo, an elephant hunt and spirals.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Cultural, economic, and settlement shifts over the last 9,000 years at Kakapel Rockshelter, Western Kenya

title: A Cemetery Where the Rich Lay Apart
place: Jebel Moya, near Sennar, southern Gezira, Sudan
text: Between about the 1st century BCE and 500 CE, herding people on the southern edge of the Meroitic world buried most of the more than 3,000 people later dug up at Jebel Moya in Sudan. The only animals placed in their graves were cattle and dogs. The 27 richest burials cluster together, with fewer poor graves than expected within about 20 m, hinting at a rule that kept them apart.

source.name: Journal of World Prehistory (PMC): Interactions and Pastoralism Along the Southern and Southeastern Frontiers of the Meroitic State, Sudan

title: Phoenician Towns With Few Phoenicians
place: Carthage and Kerkouane, Tunisia
text: Ancient DNA from Punic-era people buried at Carthage and nearby Kerkouane, in today's Tunisia, holds a surprise. None showed significant ancestry from the Phoenician homeland in the Levant. Most descended mainly from people like those of Sicily and the Aegean, many with some North African ancestry too. One Kerkouane person was a second or third cousin of someone buried at Birgi, across the sea in Sicily.

source.name: Nature (PMC): The genetic diversity of Punic people

title: The World's Largest Earthen Enclosure
place: Sungbo's Eredo, around Ijebu-Ode, Ogun State, Nigeria
text: Around the old Ijebu kingdom of southwest Nigeria, which arose in the late 1300s, runs Sungbo's Eredo: an estimated 170 km of ditches and earth banks, considered the largest earthen enclosure in the world. No one knows exactly when it was dug. Tradition says a wealthy woman named Sungbo paid for the work. Airborne laser scans of 1,000 square kilometres show it is even bigger than earlier surveys predicted.

source.name: William & Mary News: LiDAR project maps world's largest earthen enclosure

title: Indian Beads at a Nubian Shrine
place: Banganarti, near Old Dongola, Northern State, Sudan
text: Between the 800s and 1300s, Christian pilgrims came to Banganarti, a shrine of Nubia's Makuria kingdom in today's Sudan. Carnelian beads found there reveal long trade routes: chemical tests match about half to Indian sources, and others to places such as Yemen and Egypt. All were bored with diamond-tipped drills, a technique that began in ancient India. Later beads from nearby Old Dongola show the same pattern.

source.name: Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences (PMC): Carnelian ornaments from medieval upper Nubia

title: Three Steamers Struck Down by Fever
place: Confluence of the Niger and Benue rivers, Lokoja, Kogi State, Nigeria
text: In August 1841, three British steamers, the Albert, Wilberforce and Soudan, entered the Niger. Within weeks fever broke out, and as it spread they set up a model farm on Stirling Hill, where the Niger meets the Tchadda (Benue). Of 145 white crew, nearly 130 fell ill and 40 died, while only 11 of 158 Black crew got sick and none died. The Albert's surgeon ended up working the ship.

source.name: Medico-Chirurgical Review, 1843 (PMC): Medical History of the Expedition to the Niger, during the Years 1841-2

title: When Ostrich Plumes Were Gold
place: Oudtshoorn, Western Cape, South Africa
text: From around 1880, Jewish traders, mainly from Lithuania, settled in Oudtshoorn, South Africa, and helped build world markets for ostrich feathers. Max Rose, the 'ostrich feather king', arrived in 1890. In 1913 South Africa's industry peaked, with more than 775,000 birds producing a million pounds in weight of plumes for export. Then fashionable feathered hats fell out of favour, and the market crashed around World War I.

source.name: Encyclopaedia Judaica (Encyclopedia.com): Oudtshoorn

title: A Swahili Fever Name Crosses Oceans
place: Stone Town, Zanzibar, Tanzania
text: In 1870, a disabling fever with painful joints swept Zanzibar, where people called it 'kidinga pepo', pronounced something like 'denga'. James Christie, a Scottish-trained doctor serving the Sultan, argued that an 1823 East African outbreak had spread to India and the West Indies, and that both the disease and its name reached the Caribbean from Africa. Researchers today think his 1871 outbreak was chikungunya.

source.name: PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases (PMC): Comparing diagnostic methods for historical arbovirus outbreaks: Insights from 19th century dengue epidemics
